sections.overview: This northern Tasmanian crayfish is the largest freshwater crustacean known, though giant individuals are now uncommon. It belongs to an endemic genus with two smaller close relatives, A. tricornis and A. franklinii.
sections.identification: Exceptional adults can exceed 80 cm in extended length. Individuals may reach 6 kg, while 2–3 kg animals are now considered large. No standard height or width is given; males have larger front pincers than females. Its spiny body ranges from dark brown-green to black or blue. Juveniles can be separated from A. tricornis and A. franklinii by a raised ridge along the middle of the rostrum between the eyes.
sections.habitat: It is endemic to northern Tasmania, where it occupies rivers, streams and some lakes. It uses shaded waterways with pools, logs, undercut banks and native vegetation along the banks.
sections.diet: Its diet broadens with age and includes leaves and animal matter, such as small fish, when available. The sources describe an opportunistic freshwater crayfish rather than a single specialized food source.
sections.behavior: It grows very slowly and can live for as long as 60 years, so large adults represent many years of survival.
sections.reproduction: The species has low breeding potential. Females carry their attached eggs and young beneath the abdomen during brooding.
sections.ecology: This large benthic crustacean depends on clean, structurally varied streams and is vulnerable when riparian cover or water quality is degraded. Its slow growth also means local populations recover slowly after losses.
sections.conservation: It is listed as Vulnerable under Tasmanian and Australian federal legislation and is protected from fishing. Illegal capture and degradation of stream habitat remain documented threats.
